utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-PT, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today we have a Status Conference. I'd like to have the appearances. Prosecution, first.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Mr. Dan Saxon, and my name is Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff. We are accompanied by our case manager, Ms. Ana Katalinic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Mr. Seselj, you are present. You are representing yourself. Before I continue, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, first of all, I demand that you remove these spies from the courtroom, the ones that are acting as my counsel. That is the basic pre-condition for having this Status Conference held. Basic procedure is not there for as long as they are here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, my question to you simply was whether you could hear me in a language you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am telling you, Mr. Orie, that you have to throw these spies of yours out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, by your answer, I take it that you could hear my question. I now move to the presence of stand-by counsel. Could they introduce themselves.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They cannot introduce themselves because they are not the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I -- yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hooper cannot say anything on behalf of my Defence. He is your spy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I did not ask Mr. Hooper to say anything on your behalf. I asked Mr. Hooper, who is appointed as stand-by counsel with specific functions, to introduce himself, and I'll give him an opportunity to do that now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He cannot even introduce himself because he is your spy who is acting as my counsel, pretending to be my counsel. I cannot defend myself for as long as he is here. Either remove me or remove him. Both of us cannot stay on in this courtroom. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: First of all --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing, nothing, he cannot say a thing here. Nothing. He does not have the right to say anything here. He is a liar who is falsely introducing himself as my Defence counsel. He is your spy. Hooper is a spy who is hindering my defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hooper, the Chamber will adjourn for a minute at this moment, and upon our return, the Chamber will inform everyone in this courtroom about what it considered during this adjournment. We'll stand adjourned for, most likely not more than 10 minutes, so I would like everyone to stay stand-by. --- Break taken at 9.16 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume this hearing. Mr. Seselj, I'd like to bring a few matters to your attention. First of all, in an order of the 25th of October, 2006, this Trial Chamber ordered the Registrar to appoint stand-by counsel with necessary support staff to perform the functions as described in that order. Did you receive a copy of that decision in a language you understand, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not get any decision. I just got an order from the Trial Chamber that was addressed to the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the order concerning appointment of stand-by counsel and the late commencement of trial, dated the 25th of October. Are you referring to that decision, to that order?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you receive that in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I got it in the Serbian language, partly impaired Serbian language, but still Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, did you receive a copy of a decision dated the 30th of October, 2006, a decision by the Deputy Registrar, in which he decided, pursuant to the Appeals Chamber decision of the 20th of October, 2006, and the Trial Chamber's order of the 25th of October, 2006, to withdraw Mr. Hooper and Mr. O'Shea as counsel and co-counsel and to assign Mr. Hooper as stand-by counsel and Mr. O'Shea as co-counsel to Mr. Hooper, effective as of the date of that decision? Did you receive a copy of that decision, Mr. Seselj, in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you're hereby informed that if, for whatever reason, you disagree with the order or the decision, that you could seek whatever remedy that is available to you, the remedy not being interrupting Mr. Hooper if he starts speaking in this courtroom. Mr. Seselj, you have interrupted more than once when I gave an opportunity to Mr. Hooper to introduce himself. You are hereby warned that if you would interrupt again, if I give Mr. Hooper an opportunity to introduce himself, or later to speak, that the Chamber will consider this as a persistence in disruptive conduct, and that if you would persist in such disruptive conduct, that it would warrant the removal of you from this courtroom, under Rule 80(B) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. If the Chamber, which it hopes has no need to do that, if the Chamber would have to take such a decision, then it would also decide, as provided for in the order of the 25th of October and the decision of the Registrar of the 30th of October, it will, if it comes to that, instruct Mr. Hooper to temporarily take over, as provided in that decision and those orders -- in that order and that decision. Just for your information, I will quote. It's in the decision, under (H), being part of the functions to be performed by stand-by counsel in this case, "to temporarily take over the conduct of the defence from the accused should the Trial Chamber find, following a warning, that the accused is engaging in disruptive conduct or conduct requiring his removal from the courtroom, under Rule 80(B) of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence." I'll repeat what I said after I verified that you had received these orders: That if you are unhappy with them, if you want them to be reversed, that you can seek remedies that are legally open to you, not, however, to express your disagreement by disrupting conduct in this courtroom. Having said this, Mr. Hooper, you are invited to introduce yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, I demand that I be given an opportunity to state my views on your warning. It is my right to state my views on that warning. The Appeal Chamber reminded you of that as well, that I have the right to state my views before you pass a decision on removing me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, the Chamber decided that Mr. Hooper will have the opportunity first just to say who he is and that he is present in this courtroom, and then you'll have an opportunity to raise any issue about his presence after he has -- after we have on the record that Mr. Hooper is in this courtroom, accompanied by Mr. O'Shea. Mr. Hooper, would you please introduce yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: I'm David Hooper, with Andreas O'Shea, and assisted by Ms. Lea Kulinowski. And I stress this time: We do not represent this accused, Dr. Seselj. We do not represent him. And we have had no contact with him. I make that plain so that he can hear me say that, because I wondered this morning whether he may have been under the misapprehension I was here to represent him. I am not. I am here, together with Mr. O'Shea, to act as stand-by counsel, on the instruction of the Registrar, following the order of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hooper. Mr. Seselj, I understand that you wanted to raise an issue in relation to the presence of Mr. Hooper and Mr. O'Shea in this courtroom. You have the opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hooper and O'Shea filed at least ten motions on my behalf and without my approval. I have come to learn that Hooper even signed some kind of agreement with the Prosecutor, and I don't know anything about the content of that agreement. In that way, they introduced a certain practice here that does not exist in the civilised world; that someone who is imposed on behalf of the Defence without his agreement undertakes matters related to procedure. In that way, my defence becomes senseless from the very start. I demand from you that you remove either them or me from this courtroom. In this courtroom there is not enough room both for Hooper and me, and now it is up to you. Do whatever you want. My defence is impossible for as long as Hooper and O'Shea are sitting there where the Defence is supposed to sit. So even an outside observer would get that they are the ones who are representing the Defence rather than me. You can declare me insane or whatever, but you cannot do that without proper medical expertise, and it is only then that you can bring in someone who is going to play-act as my Defence counsel. It is my place to sit in the first row, because when Prosecution witnesses come in, they have to get the right impression, that I am on a footing of equality with the Prosecution. This way it's -- everything is upside down. It is psychologically unbearable for me to bear Hooper and O'Shea sitting in front of me in the courtroom. If I have to be full of anxiety in terms of what they are going to do next on my behalf, then I can't conduct my defence. There is no compromise solution here. You have to decide either to remove them or to remove me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if it's any contribution, and if it makes any difference at all, if Mr. Seselj wants to sit here and we don't mind giving up these seats to sit somewhere else convenient. May I just say, in respect of my motions that at one time were demanded of us, our understanding is those are all in abeyance in any respect, and so Mr. Seselj at this point has, as it were, a completely open field and he shouldn't feel that any previous motions that were, in fact, submitted by us, as we were directed to do, are binding on him, because I don't believe that they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hooper, seating in this courtroom is not the first issue raised by Mr. Seselj, and how to deal with any motions or submissions that have been filed by you during the period when you acted under the then relevant orders as assigned counsel is also a matter for a later stage to discuss. The first issue Mr. Seselj raised is that he seems not to accept you - and he referred to you as a person - to be appointed as his stand-by counsel. Mr. Seselj, I already informed you that, for whatever reason, including any reason concerning the person of Mr. Hooper and the way he acted in the past period, if you disagree, you can seek the remedy that's available to you. And I would say if it comes to the person of -- appointed stand-by counsel, I think it would be that you have -- you would have to address the Registrar --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Seselj, I have not finished yet. Therefore, I repeat that disrupting the order in this courtroom is not one of the remedies available to you. Then, second, I did understand your primary request for this Chamber to choose whether to remove Mr. Hooper or you from the courtroom, because, as I understood you, you could not be within this courtroom with him. Apart from seating where, that is a matter that comes second and is not of primary concern, if I understood you well. The Chamber denies your suggestion to remove Mr. Hooper, wherever seated, from this courtroom. That's the ruling on this matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, Mr. Orie, I request that I be removed from the courtroom. This is my procedural right. Because, for as long as Hooper is here, there is no room for me in the courtroom. It is impossible for me to conduct my defence. And don't you ever even bring me into the courtroom until Hooper is removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, first of all, whether it is your right to be removed from the courtroom is not, in my view, a correct understanding of the law. We will continue, and the warning stands, that if you behave in a disruptive manner, then the Chamber has warned you that this might warrant your removal, and then we'll see what happens.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, you may not continue until Hooper and O'Shea are removed from the courtroom. You cannot continue with me present here. I've said here long enough, and I'm quite surprised that you seem to initially have understood me well and now you are acting contrary to that. It is impossible for Hooper and me to be present in the same courtroom simultaneously. It is absolutely impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, your last interruption has been considered by the Chamber. You interrupted when I wanted to proceed with this Status Conference. The Chamber considers this persistence in disruptive conduct. And since you have been warned that such conduct may warrant a removal of the accused from the courtroom, the Chamber hereby decides that you will be removed from the courtroom. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hooper, in accordance with the order of the Chamber, the order of the Chamber of the 25th, under (H), the Chamber draws your attention to the fact that it belongs to your duties at this moment to temporarily take over the conduct of the defence from the accused, since the Trial Chamber has found, following the warning, that the accused is engaging in disruptive conduct and considered this conduct such that it ordered the removal of the accused from the courtroom, under Rule 80(B) of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I take it that your present position is clear to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll continue with the Status Conference. No agenda has been distributed among the parties. The Chamber has an agenda on its mind but considered it not appropriate to distribute it among the parties if no copy would be available in a language the accused, who was supposed to represent himself during this Status Conference, was available to him. I said the language the accused understands would be available to him. We have on our list, first of all, and unfortunately Mr. Seselj left the courtroom so I would have introduced to him the present composition of this Bench: Judge Robinson, sitting to my right, and Judge Hoepfel sitting to my left. I think it was by a decision of the President of yesterday that Judge Hoepfel was not only appointed for pre-trial matters but also for the trial of Mr. Seselj. First of all, I would like to inform you that the Chamber considers it, at this moment, not feasible to have a pre-trial conference following this Status Conference. The Chamber considers that we are not sufficiently ready to do that today. So we will continue with the Status Conference, and we had in mind to schedule another Status Conference next week, but the present situation might cause us to reconsider the court scheduling for the next week or even for this week. What I had on my agenda was a review of the decisions since the 20th of October, 2006. I had in mind that the Chamber would go through this decision, which we very briefly did, with the accused, and then to pay attention to the role of stand-by counsel as well. Mr. Hooper, just for a moment, forgetting about that your situation has been temporarily changed - at this moment you have taken over duties; you're conducting the defence - well, let's just assume that this is temporary and that you'd be back in your position as stand-by counsel soon. Of course we cannot predict what will happen. But are there any questions in respect of your position, if you would be stand-by counsel again, as far as your role is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. Well, let's revert entirely to stand-by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: -- stand-by counsel. Thank you. The position of stand-by counsel is wholly reactive to the wishes of the Chamber, in my understanding, and is not, in any way, proactive, not to any significant degree in any event. From time to time, there might, it seems to us, be issues that we can see that perhaps could be usefully raised in order to be discussed and resolved which could, for example, not be raised by the -- by Dr. Seselj himself. Now, of course, it might be that he's considered the particular matter and decided not to raise it. That's one obvious situation. Another situation might be that representing himself with such a feast of matters to consider, that perhaps he may have overlooked a particular aspect. You can see that at present, certainly, and I don't see the matter changing in the future, you can see at present that our relationship with Dr. Seselj is an absolute zero. There's no contact between us. So there's no situation whereby we can informally, for example, raise or discuss matters with him outside the court. So it's against that background that we wonder whether the Court has any expectation that we, in fact, become slightly proactive to the extent of raising matters which are not themselves raised by the Chamber or raised by the accused. It might be, for example, that we could sit here and consider that there could be a significant point that could be raised in the distant future, which it would be far more appropriate to raise now. And, in fact, if it had been full counsel, it would probably be our duty to raise with the Chamber so that the matter could be considered and disposed of and otherwise dealt with and reacted upon. So it's against that kind of background that we wonder what our position is. Aside from that, can you just give me one moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: That is the matter, in fact, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hooper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Aside from that, I don't think there are any other matters that arise at the moment while stand-by counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Hooper. It's not only that the Chamber doesn't expect you to raise any issue on your own behalf because you consider it to be -- to contribute to a smooth and, perhaps, fair hearing of this case. The Chamber even expects you not to do so unless specifically invited by the Chamber to address the Chamber on a certain matter or instructed to do so by Mr. Seselj, even if you would have low expectations as far as ever receiving such an instruction. That's how the Chamber interprets its own decision of the 25th of October, as far as the functions of stand-by counsel are concerned, which have been given a follow-up in the Registrar's decision to appoint you as stand-by counsel. So we take this decision literally; that is, even if, for example, Mr. Seselj would raise an issue which you could support with case law or whatever, or if there would be an issue that would materially advance the proceedings and not raised by Mr. Seselj, you not being invited by the Chamber to address the matter, the Chamber therefore expects you not, then, to raise any issue. That's how we consider your role as stand-by counsel, and, of course, Mr. O'Shea's position as stand-by co-counsel or co-stand-by counsel. I don't know how to say it. That's how the Chamber sees it. Is this clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd like to move on to what is our second point on the agenda, the second point on the agenda for us being the readiness of the parties to commence trial. Of course, we are finding ourselves in a bit of an awkward position here because I would have liked to hear from Mr. Seselj what he would still need, if anything at all, to start the trial. Mr. Hooper, could you make any observations at this moment from two points of view; that is, first of all, in the situation where Mr. Seselj would represent himself again at the start of the trial, whether you at this moment would have any observations as to what would still be needed for him to prepare for the start of the trial, and perhaps add to that what would be needed if the temporary situation would become - we don't know whether it ever will - would become a permanent situation so that the Chamber doesn't have to come back soon and ask one time, what if Mr. Seselj represents himself, what if Mr. Seselj will be represented. So the Chamber would like to be informed about your views on both situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Very well. Dealing, first of all, with Dr. Seselj's position today, towards the end of August, Dr. Seselj lost his right to represent himself and that right was only given back to him just over a week ago or so, on the 20th of October. In those circumstances, it would, in our view, be most unlikely that Dr. Seselj could be in a position to be properly prepared for his case in the near future, because he would have effectively have lost almost two months when he was, presumably mentally very much on the back foot, thinking that he wasn't in fact representing himself. Now, at this stage, also, there are a large number of motions that he needs to address his mind to and which he would not have been addressing his mind to because most of them arose, in fact, since he lost his right to self-represent; and in respect of none of them, until a week or so ago, was there any expectation that he himself would be responding. So those two matters, in a way part of the same thing, but taken together, together with the history of disclosure here, both of exhibits and of witnesses, all of which have come very late in this case, considering he's been in custody for three and a half years, suggests to us that Dr. Seselj will not be prepared to start his trial in the immediate future. In respect of the other matter, it's very difficult to wear these two hats, in a way, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd -- perhaps I could intervene. I do understand. Earlier, at a Status Conference, when, also in the absence of Mr. Seselj, the start of the trial has been discussed, and later on you have requested a, well, let's say, a slow start for the proceedings - two days a week for November; three days a week for December. Perhaps I should limit my question because I can imagine what uncomfortable feelings you'd have. If the situation in which you would represent Mr. Seselj would continue, not on a temporary basis but on a more continuous basis, is there anything that would change, in view of submissions you've made before?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Submissions in respect of response to motions, for example?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm mainly talking about the speed of the start, the pace of the trial in the early stages, and the starting moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Well, it won't come, I'm sure, as a surprise to know that the events of the last ten days or two weeks have rather taken the wind out of our sails as well. We have been effectively out of the case for ten days, coupled with which, both this week and last week, there was, on my part for example, the necessity of coming here, and every visit here is a loss of effectively the best part of two days, as you'll probably appreciate. In fact, in terms of actual attention, work paid to a case in the case of the witnesses it's not very effective or hasn't been in the past. The result of that is that any course has, I think, to be altered by the addition of about two weeks in terms of preparation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Having said that, the only other worrying concern is this: That there are significant matters in respect of motions and responses that need to be addressed, particularly, for example, in respect of early witnesses, and this -- finding oneself in this halfway house in terms of no continuum of presentation - I know, Mr. President, you can appreciate - places us, as far as us wearing that hat, in a difficult position at present. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, several times reference has been made to disclosure, well, let's say, since mid-August, of a substantive amount of material. Could you update the Chamber on -- to what extent this disclosure, and under what rule it was, whether this material has been disclosed at an earlier stage, and at what format it had been disclosed at an earlier stage, and whether it was disclosed to counsel only. I take it that this is what happened after the Registrar had appointed Mr. Hooper as counsel, up to the moment that the Appeal Chamber has reversed the Decision of this Chamber, the Appeal Chamber's Decision of the 20th of October. Could you please inform us, and could you also explain to us if there is a substantial amount of material disclosed that was not earlier disclosed, either under a Rule 92 ter motion or in any other respect, how you'd consider that the Defence - and you know the Defence is accused and counsel, so for whatever situation - would have sufficient time to prepare for that material.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the assignment of Mr. Hooper as counsel, the accused had actually received several batches of materials, according to Rule 66 and also according to Rule 68. However, as it was in electronic format mostly, he didn't use it. He rejected the acceptance of these materials. He received some Rule 68 material in hard copy, and that he kept. He received certain materials that was in English language that he did not accept. Since the assignment of Mr. Hooper as counsel, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you: Material in English, which he did not accept --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Material disclosed under what rule? Because under 66(A)(ii) and 66(B), I think the material should be disclosed in a language the accused understands, whereas Rule 68, with the exception of exculpatory material, can be disclosed in another language as well. Could you inform us about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What, actually, Mr. Seselj did was, whenever we provided materials to him, we usually provided them in both languages, B/C/S and English, and he always would exclude the English, send it back, and keep the B/C/S material, whenever it was in hard copy. And that was usually filings. For example, if we did 92 bis filings and the like, he would actually keep the B/C/S versions and send back the English. That's what I was addressing when I spoke about him sending back materials in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask one question in that respect. When you're talking about 92 bis, I take it that this is the old 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, that's the old rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Quite a substantial part of material that may have been disclosed may have been in English only, especially if I think it, all through, went to 92 bis (D), transcripts are not available in B/C/S. How was this material disclosed to him?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I have now to ask ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, when those materials were -- the English transcripts were provided and sent back by the accused. But at the same time, we proposed through the Registrar to provide audiotapes, but that option was never taken. It was actually when we make filings, it's up to the Registrar to provide the translation, and we proposed to send him audio files but that was not done, as far as we were informed. And he would have sent it back anyway because it would have been electronic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What would have been done by him is, of course, speculation --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Although one could have certain expectations. Does that mean that -- perhaps I should address the Registry in this respect as well, that any 92 bis material, and I'm specifically thinking about transcripts of other cases, were finally not offered to Mr. Seselj, not even in electronic format? The representative of the Registry, could he inform the Chamber of what happened in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do understand that the representative of the registry would need to verify some of the information he thinks is correct information, but before putting it on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I would have to double check on the exact status of those tapes -- the.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then you will have an opportunity to answer this question later on after you've had a chance to inquire with colleagues in the Registry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, I will. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there seems to be some uncertainty. Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, I interrupted you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Since the assignment of Mr. Hooper, we actually made four submissions of Rule 66 -- Rule 66 materials, and they were only sent to him and not disclosed to the accused. And it was in electronic format. If we now would have to repeat this exercise for the accused, submitting this same material to the accused, it would take us about two weeks to put it all together. It would be much easier if we could simply copy the CD-ROMs that we provided to Mr. Hooper. Then it would be a matter of a day or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are these CD-ROMs only in English?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: English and B/C/S, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: B/C/S is available. So it was disclosed at that time --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mostly statements of witnesses that we are going to call or that were of interest to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No transcripts?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Previous testimony as well and also DVDs and audios.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In what language?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The audio of previous testimony. In B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In B/C/S. So do I understand that all the material that has been recently disclosed to Mr. Hooper was accompanied by B/C/S versions of that same material.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's for the full, 100 per cent correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, of course, the Chamber will consider whether disclosure would have to be repeated for an accused who represents himself. We are temporarily in a situation where he is not, but we have to anticipate to a situation that we'd proceed on the basis as we started this morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps one more remark. In relation to Rule 68, we also provided to counsel Rule 68 material in English and B/C/S. We would have to repeat that as well, but it's not very much so that can be done in -- on very short notice, if we have to repeat that same disclosure to the accused as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So that's not significant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're saying you would need not more than two weeks to disclose anew any material which was recently disclosed to Mr. Hooper when he was acting as counsel for the situation where the -- the present situation, although temporarily interrupted, the present situation where Mr. Seselj is representing himself, and again only temporarily now interrupted by the decision of this morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But let me also mention a third issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's delayed disclosure. We have a lot of witnesses who've delayed disclosure, and there are also two motions pending to this issue. This also needs -- will have to be done at the time when we are -- have to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you give us any impression about the amount of that material? Again, are we talking mainly about statements, which are usually smaller in size, or are we talking about transcripts, which are usually huge in size?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are speaking about both. It's statements and it's also transcripts. And they all relate to our motions in relation to 92 bis and ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have to see whether we have sufficient information to have an estimate of the size of that material. Mr. Hooper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Yes. May I just add that there's the exhibits as well, all of the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All the exhibits. And all the exhibits are how many?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The exhibits related to the delayed disclosure witnesses. You can actually see it easily from our pending motions, where we always have an ex parte annex, and there you can see the statements, the transcripts, and also the related exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does is always give the number of pages, each, of the exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's difficult for us. If I have a hundred exhibits, it could be a hundred pages, but it could be 2.000 as well. So the Chamber is very much trying to form its opinion about what would be needed to prepare, to look at these materials. And these exhibits, have they been disclosed at an earlier stage?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And to what extent? Most of them? Part of them?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think most of them. If you speak about delayed disclosure witnesses, the neutral documents were disclosed. But those bearing a name and certain relevance to the witness were not disclosed. What you can see is, attached to the motions were the DVDs, that entire material including the exhibits. And when you look at the index of these materials, you can actually see the range of the ERN numbers and then you can see how many pages there are behind a certain exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That needs a lot of calculations.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider -- who is going to do those calculations?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: It is quite a lot of calculations, and some of it is unknown to us because, of course, some of these are ex parte matters and my friend there is talking about matters that haven't been served at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: But the exhibits themselves were served on us, and I mean the totality of the basic exhibits were served on the 5th or 6th of September, on us, but they wouldn't, I think, have been served on the accused. And indeed that's right. So he hasn't had any of the exhibits in this case. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless they were among the material that was offered to him before. Whether or not he then accepted it, whether he accepted them in electronic format --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: They're all on CDs, and so I'm not sure they ever were, in fact, even tendered to him. They weren't, in fact, because people calculated his reaction would be to reject them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I understood that on various occasions, Mr. Seselj refused to accept them. But, of course, that's different from not having offered them to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: That's true, but -- that's true. But from the time that, certainly, I came on the scene, I think the Prosecution viewed service on me as sufficient, given his reaction and -- his main reaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that, Mr. Hooper. But whether it has been disclosed to him at an earlier stage so that he could be -- familiarise himself already with the content of the material, now knowing that this material will be used during the examination of witnesses, that's, of course -- those are two different matters. Disclosure is one and disclosure specifically pointing at the use of that material at the testimony of a certain witness is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have not disclosed the exhibits when we filed the exhibits list because we were then waiting for a decision on the form of disclosure. And when this decision was taken, we put everything together and wanted to provide it to Mr. Seselj, but then Mr. Hooper was assigned and so we gave it only to Mr. Hooper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it took you from the 4th of July until, what was it, mid-August?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, because it was a huge amount of exhibits. So he didn't get them. It's only with Mr. Hooper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll consider that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there anything else, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, that you'd like to raise in relation to disclosure issues at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think what the Chamber would need is a clear, concise overview of what has been disclosed, offered, not accepted, what language, what format, so that we have, for once and forever, that we know exactly the facts on which will have to base our decisions. Similarly, I am now addressing the representative of the Registry, the Chamber would also like to be informed in detail about what facilities were given to Mr. Seselj as far as computers offered to him, assistance in training, people stand-by available to Mr. Seselj in the Detention Unit to provide access to material, even if he would not have accepted it and therefore not received it. But the Chamber would like to know what exactly facilities were available to him in order to be in a better position to see what opportunities he has had to look at these materials and to what extent he was not in a position to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Mr. President, can we raise one other matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me first finish. One second.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask the Registry how many days you could prepare a -- perhaps a short memo on this to be distributed among the parties which, perhaps, would have attached any communications in writing on the matter? How much time would you need to prepare for that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this will require me to be in touch with the United Nations Detention Unit and the Office of the Legal Aid and Detention, and I would anticipate having a response to you tomorrow, by close of business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber would appreciate it if you would provide us with such a survey. Mr. Hooper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Maybe a further matter that could also be addressed by the Registry is what facilities, or whether adequate facilities have been provided to Dr. Seselj in terms of the investigation of his case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you include that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's taken note of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be good, also, to be aware of any further thoughts developed within the Registry on facilities to be given to Mr. Seselj, what facilities to provide to him or what facilities he asked for specifically. Of course, we have some information from the past, but we have no update on whether he recently asked for further matters, and it's important for the Chamber, to assess the preparedness of Prosecution and Defence, to have this information available.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there- let me just go back to my agenda- any other matter to be raised in relation to preparation for trial, preparedness, and disclosure? Madam Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would like to refer to our letter to the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a second. The Chamber is aware that you sent a letter -- well, you're referring to it in open court, although you said the letter was confidential. I don't know whether it's about the existence of that letter or whether it was some aspects of the content that should be dealt in a confidential way. The Chamber noted that this letter was sent to the Chamber, copied to the accused, but the Chamber is not aware of any translation provided to him. So, just for the record, and anticipating a situation that the taking over of Mr. Hooper is on a temporary basis, I would like you to introduce any matter contained in that letter that we have not dealt with now, orally.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually, Mr. Seselj did receive the letter in a language he understands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber wasn't aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We had a translation going with it, and also we provided a copy to stand-by counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, that doesn't need, then, the confidentiality of the matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The confidentiality related to one witness issue, that was point 3, and I wouldn't actually -- I would not raise it here. I only want to mention the witness scheduling, and I have already mentioned in the letter that we need sufficient advance notice of the trial date where the witnesses have to be appear, and we think the -- we and the witness -- Victims and Witnesses Unit would need two weeks so that we know in advance two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We also addressed in this letter that we consider to change the witness order back to the original, starting with the insiders. We have actually -- we have actually taken now a different view, because if we would do that, it would cause a considerable delay because of these delayed disclosure issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Therefore, we have decided that we will go along according to the revised order, starting with one insider and then having crime-base witnesses for the following weeks. That's what I actually want to bring to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You address a matter, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, which the Chamber considered already with some concern, because if you would have moved back to your original schedule, then it might have caused the Chamber to further delay the calling of these witnesses in order to give additional time for preparation, in view of disclosure. That's also the reason why we want to be informed in such detail about disclosure issues, late disclosure, the form of disclosure, et cetera. But I do understand now that, whether we'd start in the present situation, although temporarily interrupted, that Mr. Seselj represents himself, or whether we start -- we would have started in the situation war Mr. Hooper would represent Mr. Seselj, that the order of calling witnesses would not be different.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that information. I'm looking at the clock -- yes, Mr. Hooper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we don't know at present, of course, how long "temporary" is and, in particular, what the position is in respect of necessary response to motions, decisions in respect of those motions being, of course, quite crucial to the way in which the case unfolds, and in particular with respect to the first and subsequent witnesses, who are rather loosely described as crime-base but rather go more pointedly to the accused than certainly what one's general conception of crime base might imply. I don't know whether, speaking here essentially as stand-by counsel, it would at all assist you and the future of this case, whether you were, in fact, to have a Status Conference, as it were, where Dr. Seselj attended and we did not. I can see, of course, certain difficulties that might arise because of that. But there's no way for me to gauge the full reaction, as it were, of this accused, and the only conduit for that is through the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can I say I would not be in a position to accept that course. The procedures here are not to be determined by the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: I do very much appreciate that position, Judge Robinson, very much so. But, as I say, as stand-by counsel with a common interest in the interests of the accused, or his perception of interests, it's -- perhaps nevertheless remains a possibility, that without him determining what this Chamber does, and being quite clear on that, nevertheless there may be an opportunity for at least him to express particular views which, for some reason, he feels unable to express - he's expressed already - with my presence. But that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The point is that you have been appointed, and quite properly appointed. If he has a difficulty with that, then he must pursue whatever remedies are open to him under the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Yes. I think that was made very clear to him this morning. That merely takes time, and if it's, to some extent, a gauging of an opinion, an explanation, I'm merely saying that we, for our part, won't feel slighted in any way if, in fact, that other course were taken. I make that absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What would be slighted in my view, would not be you but the dignity and prestige of the Chamber, of the Tribunal, were that course to be followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the Chamber appreciates that you raised the issue. Judge Robinson expressed already clearly that it's a course that he would not support, and of course the Chamber will consider whatever you have raised and-- to see how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Mr. O'Shea points out one final matter, and that's an issue of new deadlines for motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: But there's quite a lot there and we may need time to reflect on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What I'd like to do is adjourn for a break which is a little longer than usual so that the Chamber has an opportunity to consider a few matters during this break, and then to resume ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To resume at 11.30. I inform the parties, meanwhile that, on my agenda, the one remaining point was to inform the accused of what has been said during the 65 ter Conference as far as what the Chamber anticipates might be its decision on the -- on the reduction of the indictment. Of course, there's no need at this moment to raise the issue in the absence of the accused, although we might decide that we'll just read, for the record, the most important part so that at least there's an opportunity, perhaps at a later stage - I don't know whether that will materialise or not - for the accused to listen to it or have only those 10 or 20 lines translated for him. I'm not the master of all the practicalities and I'm not in control of everything that should be given to him if he's not formally entitled to it. But we might decide to do that. That was on my agenda. Then the other items would be the accused's health and conditions of detention. Of course, the Chamber would have preferred to hear this from the accused himself rather than in any indirect way. But nevertheless, if there's anything to be said about it, then the parties are invited to do so. Another matter which was on the agenda: To inform Mr. Seselj about the presentation of documents in court, to explain to him that we'll use the e-court system but that he would not have to suffer under it. He'd just have to adapt the presentation of documents in such a way that they could be scanned and they could be used for e-court purposes. There's no need, I take it, to give a lot of attention to it, since at this moment the parties are aware of how the e-court system functions and instructions for the accused, perhaps, could be better given at another occasion. This also is related to the issue of facilities given to the accused. But it's mainly instructing the accused on how to present whatever he would like to tender in evidence, mainly exhibits. Are there any other matters, before we adjourn, the parties would like to add to the agenda so that the Chamber could include them in its considerations during the break?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hooper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn and resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered the present situation, the present situation being that Mr. Hooper has taken over, on a temporary basis, the defence. Since this is only on a temporary basis, the Chamber primarily considers how to proceed if this temporary situation would be ended, and therefore the Chamber is very much interested to know from Mr. Seselj himself about his preparedness for trial, because the Chamber did not receive that information today. Therefore, the Chamber will issue a Scheduling Order and would preferably have in that Scheduling Order that we'll have another Status Conference this Friday. Of course, we have to look at availability of courtrooms and teams to assist us, technical teams and interpreters, so therefore time and courtroom cannot be announced yet. We do not know whether it will be feasible at all to do that on Friday, but that's what we're aiming at. And then to restart, or to start, that Status Conference, having ended the temporary situation in which Mr. Hooper has taken over, and then see whether the Chamber can receive the information it needs to make further determinations as to when the trial could start, based upon other matters, on the information it hopes to receive from Mr. Seselj. If the Chamber will not receive that information from Mr. Seselj at the Status Conference, the Chamber will then consider again how to proceed. That's not yet a ruling but in anticipation of the Scheduling Order issued preferable today, what the Chamber has in mind. Before the break we briefly looked at any remaining agenda points. I then indicated that the Chamber, of course, would like to receive further observations, and of course we'll repeat that at the next Status Conference, on the accused's health, on conditions of detention, from Mr. Seselj himself. But, Mr. Hooper, if there's anything you would like to raise in this respect, having temporarily taken over the defence, you have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: No, there's nothing. But I'm sure the Scheduling Order and request will be translated into Serbian and provided very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take care of that. With the utmost urgency, the order will be provided. But also this Chamber is dependent on CLSS resources, but we hope we will be in a position to have it translated not later than tomorrow, or even today. Is there any other matter you'd like to raise, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. First, one information. We have meanwhile -- there is a secondary tool to go through the exhibits list to find out how many pages there are. It's not very accurate, but according to our findings, it's that the exhibits list has actually 35.000 pages, B/C/S documents, including, of course, photos, sketches, charts, and these kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would that --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That actually amounts to 40.000 pages, English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And would that include any transcripts to be tendered under Rule ...

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: As exhibits, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as exhibits. Is there any way -- because you may have noticed that the Chamber is interested to know -- I mean, what we have to do with the 92 -- old 92 bis, or new 92 ter, material, is what time to be given for preparation is still to be considered. But we know that that's the bulky material. What, then, remains is the statements, photos, so everything but excluding the transcripts, which often are hundreds and hundreds of pages? What would then remain, apart from -- because, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, at a certain moment, you and perhaps the Chamber would also have to consider whether it becomes more efficient to have a witness in court for three or four hours to repeat some of his evidence, perhaps partly on the basis of 89(F) in order to avoid that we have to read a thousand pages of transcript, of which perhaps 200 are of great relevance for the case. So we'll have to consider that, and therefore I'm emphasising again and again, what is transcript material, which is known to be always bulky material, and what is statements, documents, reports, photographs, maps, et cetera? Is there anything you can say about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I can't do that, because it's just the exhibits I've just referred to. And in this exhibits list, we have these packages, 92 bis packages. It's just mentioned as a position and not with page numbers. So we couldn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps if you could prepare for the next Status Conference, to see whether we can get some more information about that, because it might be of importance for the Chamber to -- for any determination of the further proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I just endorse what the Presiding Judge said about that, because the whole purpose of the transcript procedure is to achieve expeditiousness. And if, in this particular instance, it is not achieving that, and if, in this particular instance, it would be more expeditious to have the witness testify in court on the basis of a statement under 89(F) and be available for cross-examination, if that is the decision, then I think that is something which you should consider.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. We will do that. But I will also -- I can actually say that many of the 92 -- many of the transcripts come from the Milosevic case, and actually what we have there is a very brief cross-examination, more or less, and the -- and the tendered statement. Do you see what I mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then the -- but then it's not bulky material anymore. That's exactly what I wanted to find out. To what extent these, what I'd say, old 92 bis material is bulky material, because if we're talking about 30.000, 35.000 - in English 40.000 - pages, then I'd very much like to know whether we're talking about 2.000 pages of documents, maps, statements, et cetera, and 33.000 pages of 92 bis (D) material, or whether the balance is different. Because, as just explained by Judge Robinson, if the bulky material would require such an enormous time for further preparation, both the Bench, perhaps the Defence, then at a certain moment we should consider what is the most expeditious way of proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether it's to proceed under 92 bis or 92 ter road or to, perhaps, differentiate and say here the material is not bulky, it's easy to prepare for that, so we could consider admission of that material under Rule 92, et cetera; and perhaps for others to say this material is so bulky, so just hearing the testimony will be far more expeditious and far more easy to digest than to have it all prepared on the basis of this bulky 92 bis material.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This is understood, Your Honour, and we will do that. The other thing I wanted to inform you about: In the past, we have actually filed four disclosure reports detailing what was provided to the accused and what -- what was his reaction to this, whether he took it or rejected it, and that covers the years 2003 and most of 2004. Do you want us to repeat this information in our now new disclosure report, or could we simply cover now the time period from October 2004 to today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If it would be easy either for us or for you to link the information in these old reports to recent disclosure, then there should be not a major problem, either for you or for us. We might ask you -- we might not yet ask you to link it and see whether we can do it without too many problems. If it becomes problematic, we might invite you to say, Well, show us exactly what, in this report, on that disclosure, whether it's linked or it's the same material. I have not every recent disclosure in my mind. But please check whether it's easy to link it, easy to make -- to see whether the recent disclosure is already part of earlier disclosed material which -- and also whether the information, whether he accepted or did not accept it, whether it was prior to the 4th of July decision; whether it was after the 4th of July decision, so that's the format. So that's all clear so we have a very transparent picture of what is new, what was rejected, what was accepted, what was known to the accused, what was not known to the accused, in what format it was brought to the attention of the accused, so we have a clear picture of that --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because that's our major concern at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Anything else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Finally, the Chamber would ask the Registry to provide the B/C/S audio of this Status Conference to the accused and to verify whether the necessary facilities to listen to this audio are available to the accused so that he can -- has effective access to that audio material, preferably to be prepared today. If not, the Chamber would like to be informed when it will be provided to him.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Chamber will be appraised of the status of this particular Status Conference in its audio format, or if the Chamber would also prefer, if we can have a VHS tape in the B/C/S language provided to the accused, the Chamber would be acceptable, because we ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The concern of the Chamber is that the accused has access to what has been said during this Status Conference. If he would be provided with a VHS in B/C/S, then, of course, he would be able to look at it as well, which is not essential for the Chamber, but the Chamber does not oppose, as long as he has effective access to whatever has been said during this Status Conference, be it audio, be it VHS; both fine, as long as he can --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- hear it. And if it is a video, then at least he has an opportunity to see it as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Chamber's ruling is duly considered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any other matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that that's all the information the Chamber has requested, both from Registry and the Prosecution, that it's clear what is expected, that is, the information about facilities offered to him, unless you'd like to give that information right away.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, during the break, I've had the opportunity to consult staff at the Office of Legal Aid and Detention, and we've been informed that to put together a comprehensive report, as the Chamber requested, they're requesting that the Chamber consider that report be filed sometime early next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I -- if at least the basic information would be available, even if not in its final written form, at the next Status Conference, that be highly appreciated, because otherwise we might get stuck there.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will indicate this to the concerned authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hooper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: May I mention one matter, because we may not get an opportunity to mention it again, and it's merely this: I think as an earlier stage we may have indicated our response to the question of submitting statements rather than having oral testimony from the witness. And since then, I think we've been overtaken by a change in the rules, in 92 ter, of course. And just basically in terms of our position now, we just say that. Generally, it's our view that that would have a radical effect -- or there is a radical effect on that, on the interpretation of that rule, when you have a defendant who's representing himself and who may not, therefore, be skilled in cross-examination. It's another factor to take into account. And also, that that is a particular matter, because it concerns, for example, the first witness the Prosecution intend to call, VS-017, it's a particular matter that is imminent, needs to be addressed. And Dr. Seselj really, perhaps, needs to focus, perhaps, on that particular aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider this change in the Rules and the effect it will have on the self-representation of Mr. Seselj, and if need be, we'll raise the matter in his presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will consider the matter seriously and see what attention should be paid to it, either at the next Status Conference or at any other moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll adjourn until the next Status Conference of which the date, time, and courtroom are not determined yet.
